1 · Title of monograph

Alpha-1 Proteinase Inhibitor

2 · Abstract

Alpha-1 Proteinase Inhibitor (A1PI), also known as alpha-1 antitrypsin (AAT), is a human plasma-derived protein replacement therapy indicated for chronic augmentation and maintenance therapy in adults with severe hereditary A1PI deficiency and clinically evident pulmonary emphysema. Hereditary AAT deficiency arises from pathogenic variants in the SERPINA1 gene, resulting in severely diminished circulating antiprotease levels or functionally abnormal protein synthesis.

Under physiological conditions, A1PI neutralizes neutrophil elastase, a potent serine protease released by activated leukocytes in the lung, thereby protecting lung elastin and preserving alveolar wall integrity. In severe deficiency states, unopposed elastase activity accelerates connective tissue degradation and promotes panacinar emphysema.

Chronic intravenous augmentation therapy with A1PI (standard regimen: 60 mg/kg IV once weekly) restores circulating and lung tissue antiprotease concentrations above the critical protective threshold. Clinical evidence suggests that intravenous augmentation therapy may slow CT-measured lung-density loss. However, the primary combined endpoint in the RAPID trial did not reach statistical significance, and benefits on mortality and exacerbations remain uncertain.

This monograph reviews the pharmacology, clinical pharmacokinetics, therapeutic indications, safety, monitoring and guideline-based place in therapy of human A1PI augmentation products (Prolastin-C, Aralast NP, Glassia and Zemaira).

Front matter
Key summaryA1PI replacement therapy may slow pulmonary tissue destruction in severe hereditary deficiency but does not reverse existing alveolar damage, treat hepatic protein accumulation, or replace standard COPD management.

Monograph summary

4 · Monograph summary

Section 1 · Drug overview & available products. A1PI (Human) is a plasma-derived enzyme replacement therapy classed as a serine protease inhibitor (SERPIN). FDA-approved products include Prolastin-C, Aralast NP and Zemaira (lyophilized powders for reconstitution) and Glassia and Prolastin-C Liquid (ready-to-use liquids). IV augmentation replaces circulating protein but does not correct the genetic mutation or liver disease.

Section 2 · Mechanism of action. A1PI neutralizes neutrophil elastase, preserving elastin and alveolar structure. In severe AATD, unopposed elastase activity destroys alveolar walls and reduces elastic recoil. Exogenous A1PI binds neutrophil elastase via its reactive center loop, forming a stable inhibitory complex that halts proteolytic degradation.

Section 3 · Pharmacokinetics (ADME). Given by IV infusion directly into the systemic circulation. Distributes into extravascular spaces, including pulmonary interstitial and alveolar compartments. Catabolized through normal protein degradation pathways without CYP450 involvement. Mean terminal half-life of 4 to 7 days supports weekly administration.

Section 4 · Dosing & administration. Standard adult dose is 60 mg/kg IV once weekly across all FDA-labeled products. Infusion rates vary by formulation (maximum 0.2 mL/kg/min for Aralast NP and Glassia; about 0.08 mL/kg/min for Prolastin-C and Zemaira). Pediatric efficacy and renal or hepatic dose adjustments are not established. Preparation requires aseptic technique, solution inspection and a dedicated IV line without co-mixing.

Section 5 · Indications & limitations. FDA-approved for chronic augmentation in adults with severe hereditary AAT deficiency (typically serum AAT <11 μmol/L) and clinically evident emphysema. Off-label use includes necrotizing panniculitis. Not indicated without severe deficiency, for AATD-associated liver disease, or for COPD unrelated to AAT deficiency.

Section 6 · Contraindications & safety warnings. Contraindicated in IgA deficiency with antibodies against IgA (risk of severe anaphylaxis) and after prior severe systemic hypersensitivity to A1PI. As a plasma-derived agent, a theoretical residual risk of infectious-agent transmission remains despite donor screening and viral inactivation.

Section 7 · Adverse reactions. Common reactions (≥5% of subjects) include headache, upper respiratory tract infection, musculoskeletal discomfort, puncture-site bruising, nausea, fatigue and rhinitis. Serious events include anaphylaxis and severe systemic infusion reactions requiring immediate discontinuation.

Section 8 · Drug interactions. No established cytochrome P450 interactions. The main concern is physical IV incompatibility: A1PI must not be mixed with other drugs or diluents in the same infusion container.

Section 9 · Monitoring framework. Baseline serum AAT, SERPINA1 genotype/phenotype and spirometry (FEV1, FVC, DLCO). Routine monitoring covers annual pulmonary function tests, vital signs during infusions, liver function tests when indicated, and adherence and smoking status. Serial trough AAT levels and routine chest CT solely for monitoring are not recommended.

Section 10 · Clinical pearls & counseling. Confirm severe hereditary deficiency before starting; explain that treatment slows progression but cannot regenerate destroyed alveolar tissue; insist on smoking cessation; keep influenza and pneumococcal immunizations up to date.

Section 11 · Place in therapy & evidence. Guided by the 2016 COPD Foundation and 2025 Canadian Thoracic Society recommendations for non-smoking patients with severe deficiency (FEV1 ≤65–80% predicted). The RAPID trial (2015) suggested slower CT lung-density loss, although its primary combined endpoint was not statistically significant. The 2026 Cochrane review rates the evidence on mortality and exacerbations as low certainty.

Section 12 · References. Nineteen sources in Vancouver style, led by the FDA product labels and the COPD Foundation guideline. See page .

A1PI restores antiprotease balance in the lung

Section 02 · Mechanism

Normal physiological mechanism

  1. Alpha-1 antitrypsin is synthesized mainly by hepatocytes and released into the systemic circulation.
  2. It reaches the pulmonary interstitial and alveolar compartments.
  3. It inhibits neutrophil elastase, a proteolytic enzyme released by activated neutrophils.
  4. This limits degradation of elastin and other parts of the alveolar extracellular matrix.
  5. It helps maintain the structural integrity and elasticity of lung tissue.
Section 02 · Mechanism

Pharmacological mechanism

Administered A1PI raises circulating and pulmonary AAT concentrations, restoring antiprotease protection and reducing neutrophil elastase-mediated destruction of lung tissue. A1PI binds neutrophil elastase through its reactive center loop, forming a stable inhibitory complex.

Clinical significanceThe principal therapeutic objective is to slow emphysema progression by reducing proteolytic damage. Treatment does not regenerate alveolar tissue that has already been destroyed.
Section 03

3. Pharmacokinetics (ADME)

ParameterDescription
AbsorptionNot applicable in the conventional sense; given directly into the systemic circulation by IV infusion.
DistributionFrom plasma into extravascular tissues, including the pulmonary interstitial and alveolar compartments.
MetabolismCatabolized through normal protein metabolic pathways; no conventional CYP450-mediated metabolism.
ExcretionDegraded into peptides and amino acids, which enter normal metabolic pathways.
Half-lifeProduct-dependent; approximately 4–7 days in reported studies.

After IV administration, serum A1PI concentration rises rapidly. Repeated weekly administration maintains higher trough concentrations. Half-life varies between formulations and study populations; Aralast NP reported a mean terminal half-life of about 4.7 days in its comparative pharmacokinetic study. [2,5]

Clinical relevanceThe relatively long half-life supports once-weekly dosing rather than daily administration.
Evidence limitationDetailed human ADME parameters are not uniformly reported across formulations. Distribution volumes, clearance values and renal excretion percentages should not be assumed identical across products.

Adult dosage

Standard labeled augmentation dose: 60 mg/kg intravenously once weekly. Confirm the current prescribing information for the selected product. [2–5]

Example · 70 kg patient60 mg/kg × 70 kg = 4,200 mg (4.2 g) once weekly

Product-specific administration

ProductPreparationInfusion rate
Aralast NPReconstituted powderMaximum 0.2 mL/kg/min
Prolastin-CReconstituted powder0.08 mL/kg/min
Prolastin-C LiquidReady-to-use solution0.08 mL/kg/min
GlassiaReady-to-use solutionMaximum 0.2 mL/kg/min
ZemairaReconstituted powderAbout 0.08 mL/kg/min

The current product-specific prescribing information takes precedence over this summary. Do not assume identical infusion rates or preparation instructions. [2–5, 19]

Pediatric dosage

Safety and effectiveness have not been established in pediatric patients in U.S. product labeling. Routine pediatric use is therefore not established; specialist assessment is required if treatment outside the labeled adult population is considered.

Sections 04–05

Renal and hepatic impairment

  • Renal impairment: no specific dose-adjustment regimen is established in the prescribing information; clinical evidence in significant renal impairment is limited.
  • Hepatic impairment: no specific dose-adjustment regimen is established. Administered A1PI replaces circulating protein but does not correct intracellular accumulation of abnormal AAT in hepatocytes.

Administration guidelines

  1. Administer by the intravenous route only.
  2. Use aseptic technique during preparation.
  3. Inspect the solution for discoloration and visible particles.
  4. Do not mix with other medicinal products.
  5. Use the infusion filter, if required, as specified in the product label.
  6. Monitor during infusion for hypersensitivity reactions.
  7. Slow or stop the infusion if an adverse infusion reaction occurs.
  8. Follow product-specific storage and post-reconstitution handling instructions.

Section 05 · Indications

FDA-approved indication

Chronic augmentation and maintenance therapy in adults with severe hereditary Alpha-1 Proteinase Inhibitor deficiency and clinically evident emphysema.

The purpose is to increase circulating and pulmonary A1PI levels and protect against neutrophil elastase-mediated lung destruction. [2–5]

Patient selection

  • Confirmed severe hereditary AAT deficiency.
  • Evidence of emphysema.
  • Significantly reduced serum AAT concentration; a threshold below 11 μmol/L is commonly used in guideline-based selection.
  • Appropriate clinical assessment of pulmonary disease, genotype or phenotype, and serum AAT level.

Off-label use

Necrotizing panniculitis is a rare inflammatory skin manifestation associated with AAT deficiency. A1PI augmentation has been used in selected patients, but this is not a standard FDA-approved indication for the products discussed. Evidence comes mainly from case reports and small clinical experiences.

Important limitations

  • Not indicated for patients without established severe AAT deficiency.
  • Not indicated to treat AATD-associated liver disease.
  • Not indicated for routine COPD unrelated to AAT deficiency.
  • Does not reverse established alveolar destruction.

Plasma-derived product warningBecause A1PI products are derived from human plasma, there is a potential residual risk of transmitting infectious agents. Donor screening and manufacturing steps that inactivate or remove viruses reduce, but cannot completely eliminate, this risk. [2–5]

Monitorstop infusion if severe reaction

Adverse effects are generally related to infusion reactions, hypersensitivity or the individual product. The frequencies below are product-specific and should not be compared directly, because the clinical trials differed in design and sample size.

Reported adverse reactions by product

ProductReported adverse reactions / frequency
Aralast NPHeadache, musculoskeletal discomfort, puncture-site bruising, nausea and rhinorrhea in at least 5% of infusions in clinical studies. A crossover study reported headache 16%, musculoskeletal discomfort 16%, puncture-site bruising 8% and nausea 8% of infusions.
Prolastin-CUpper respiratory tract infection in more than 5% of subjects; one comparative study reported 12.5%.
Prolastin-C LiquidDiarrhea and fatigue, each in 2 of 32 subjects (6%). [19]
GlassiaHeadache and upper respiratory infection were among the common reactions; one comparative trial reported each in 9% of subjects.
ZemairaHeadache, sinusitis, upper respiratory infection, bronchitis, asthenia, increased cough, fever, injection-site hemorrhage, rhinitis, sore throat and vasodilation in at least 5% of subjects across pre-licensure studies.

Source: individual prescribing information and product clinical studies. [2–5, 19]

Sections 07–08

Serious adverse effects

Anaphylaxis and severe hypersensitivity

  • May present with urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm, hypotension or respiratory distress.
  • Requires immediate discontinuation of the infusion and emergency management.
  • Patients with IgA deficiency and anti-IgA antibodies need particular attention.

Other important reactions

  • Urticaria, angioedema, flushing, dyspnea and vomiting have been reported.
  • Postmarketing reports may not allow reliable incidence estimates because the number of exposed patients is uncertain.
Clinical actionStop the infusion and assess immediately if severe hypersensitivity or anaphylaxis is suspected. Follow institutional emergency protocols and the product label.

8. Drug Interactions

A1PIa plasma protein
→
No establishedCYP450 interaction pathway
Main practical concernIV incompatibility
→
Do not mixwith other medicines; follow label

No well-established, clinically significant pharmacokinetic drug interactions have been identified. This fits its nature as a plasma-derived protein rather than a small molecule metabolized by CYP450 enzymes.

Sections 08–09
Potential interactionMechanism / significanceManagement
Other IV medicationsPhysical incompatibility may occur if mixed in the same solution.Do not mix; give separately and follow product instructions.
Other plasma-derived productsNo established PK interaction; additive infusion reactions may complicate assessment.Monitor and follow administration instructions.
Immuno­suppressive drugsNo established clinically significant interaction.No routine dose adjustment; assess individually.
VaccinesNo established direct drug interaction.Follow routine immunization advice for AATD.
Clinical significanceThe main practical issue is IV compatibility, not a known metabolic interaction. Do not mix A1PI with other medicinal products or diluting solutions unless the product instructions specifically permit it.

Evidence limitation: formal drug-interaction studies are limited. Absence of reported interactions does not establish that every possible combination is safe.

Section 09 · Monitoring

Laboratory monitoring

ParameterPurpose
Serum AAT concentrationEstablishes deficiency and supports diagnosis.
SERPINA1 genotype / phenotypeConfirms the underlying hereditary deficiency.
Liver function tests (ALT, AST, bilirubin, ALP)Monitor associated liver disease.
Albumin and INRAssess hepatic synthetic function when liver disease is suspected.
Complete blood countGeneral assessment when clinically indicated.

Routine measurement of AAT trough concentrations to adjust augmentation doses is not generally recommended by the 2016 COPD Foundation guideline. [6]

Pulmonary monitoring

  • Spirometry, including FEV1 and FVC.
  • Diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide (DLCO).
  • Dyspnea and exercise tolerance.
  • Frequency of respiratory exacerbations.
  • Oxygen saturation when indicated.

Annual pulmonary function assessment is recommended in adults with AATD. [6]

During infusion

  • Blood pressure, heart rate and respiratory rate.
  • Oxygen saturation and temperature when indicated.
  • Signs and symptoms of infusion reactions or hypersensitivity.
Sections 09–10

Clinical assessment

  • New or worsening respiratory symptoms.
  • Signs of hypersensitivity or infection.
  • Liver-related symptoms such as jaundice or abdominal swelling.
  • Adherence to weekly treatment.
  • Smoking status and exposure to environmental irritants.
Clinical pearlRoutine serial chest CT is not recommended solely to monitor emphysema progression, because of radiation exposure. CT may be appropriate for baseline assessment in selected patients. [6]

Section 10 · Clinical pearls

Practical tips for healthcare professionals

  1. Confirm severe hereditary AAT deficiency before starting treatment.
  2. Review IgA deficiency and anti-IgA antibody history as directed by the product label and clinical context.
  3. Choose the formulation based on availability, administration requirements and patient circumstances.
  4. Use the standard 60 mg/kg weekly dose unless a specialist decides otherwise.
  5. Do not assume that a higher dose provides additional clinical benefit.
  6. Do not use augmentation therapy as a substitute for standard COPD management.
  7. Encourage smoking cessation and avoidance of occupational inhalational exposures.
  8. Assess vaccination status and provide appropriate respiratory infection prevention.

Patient counseling

  • Attend scheduled weekly infusions.
  • Report rash, itching, difficulty breathing or swelling immediately.
  • Report fever or symptoms of possible infection.
  • Avoid smoking and secondhand smoke exposure.
  • Keep up regular pulmonary follow-up.
  • Understand that treatment aims to slow further lung damage, not reverse existing emphysema.
Section 10 · Clinical pearls

Special populations

PopulationConsiderations
PregnancyAdequate controlled studies are lacking. Use only when clinically justified after specialist assessment.
BreastfeedingInsufficient data on presence in human milk or effects on the infant.
Geriatric patientsClinical trials included limited numbers of older patients; individualize treatment.
Liver diseaseAugmentation does not correct intracellular accumulation of abnormal AAT in hepatocytes and is not a treatment for AATD-associated liver disease.

Sources: individual product prescribing information. [2–5]

11. Place in Therapy

AATD + emphysemaeligible patient
→
Augmentation therapywhen appropriate
Standard COPD carefor all, as indicated
→
Integrated careand follow-up

Position in treatment guidelines

A1PI is a disease-specific augmentation treatment for selected patients with severe hereditary AAT deficiency and emphysema. It is not recommended for every patient with COPD.

2016 COPD Foundation guideline

Recommends IV augmentation for individuals with AATD-related lung disease and FEV1 at or below 65% predicted. For FEV1 above 65%, benefits, treatment burden, cost and uncertainty of evidence should be discussed individually. Augmentation is not recommended in patients who continue to smoke, those with the MZ genotype, or those with AATD-related liver disease. [6]

2025 Canadian Thoracic Society guideline

Conditionally recommends offering augmentation to selected nonsmokers or former smokers with COPD and emphysema, FEV1 below 80% predicted, a documented severe deficiency genotype and serum AAT below 11 μmol/L (0.57 g/L), while on optimal pharmacological and non-pharmacological COPD treatment. Patient selection remains important. [7]

Section 11 · Place in therapy

Clinical evidence: RAPID trial (2015)

Study featureDetails
DesignRandomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial.
Population180 participants with severe AAT deficiency.
InterventionWeekly IV A1PI 60 mg/kg versus placebo for 24 months.
Primary findingsThe combined CT lung-density endpoint did not reach statistical significance (p=0.06). At total lung capacity alone, lung-density loss was significantly slower with treatment (p=0.03).
InterpretationSupports a protective effect on lung tissue, but does not show reversal of emphysema or improvement in every clinical outcome.

Reference: Chapman et al. [8]

2026 Cochrane review

The 2026 Cochrane systematic review included six randomized studies with 526 participants. It concluded that IV augmentation therapy may make little or no difference to all-cause mortality, may slightly increase the annual rate of respiratory exacerbations, and has uncertain effects on serious adverse events. Certainty of evidence for several outcomes was low, reflecting small studies and imprecision. [9]

Section 11 · Place in therapy

When to use versus alternatives

Clinical situationSuggested approach
Severe hereditary AAT deficiency with emphysemaConsider IV augmentation therapy in eligible patients.
Mild AAT deficiency without emphysemaRoutine augmentation is not indicated.
AATD patient who continues smokingPrioritize smoking cessation; the 2016 guideline does not recommend augmentation in continuing smokers.
AATD-associated liver diseaseManage liver disease separately; augmentation is not a hepatic treatment.
COPD without severe AAT deficiencyStandard COPD treatment; no routine A1PI augmentation.

Complementary management

  • Smoking cessation and avoidance of secondhand smoke.
  • Long-acting bronchodilators (LABA and/or LAMA), as clinically indicated.
  • Inhaled corticosteroids in appropriately selected COPD patients.
  • Pulmonary rehabilitation and vaccination.
  • Supplemental oxygen when indicated.
  • Lung transplantation in selected patients with advanced disease.
Overall clinical judgmentA1PI augmentation is a targeted treatment for carefully selected patients with severe hereditary AAT deficiency and emphysema. Its strongest evidence concerns preservation of CT-measured lung density; effects on mortality, exacerbations and quality of life remain less certain.

Drug Information Course · PP 707

Key take-home message

A1PI augmentation therapy slows the progression of emphysema in adults with severe hereditary AAT deficiency. It does not reverse existing lung damage or treat AATD-related liver disease, and it does not replace standard COPD care.

  • Smoking cessation is essential.
  • Keep influenza and pneumococcal vaccinations up to date.
  • Annual pulmonary function follow-up.
